strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: first large-scale long-term RVOS dataset with 2,193 videos averaging 60+ seconds, compared to existing datasets with only 4-13 second clips

Comprehensive and well-curated dataset: 24,689 text descriptions, 2.1M masks, 163 object categories, diverse sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), with rigorous annotation workflow including validation and iterative correction
Well-motivated evaluation metrics: tIoU and vIoU address practical limitations of per-frame metrics by assessing temporal consistency and the ability to predict object absence

Thorough benchmarking demonstrating clear challenges: 6 SOTA methods evaluated consistently; oracle analysis reveals ~25% performance gap (52.8-54.5 vs 77.3-80.6 J&F) demonstrating long-video challenges
Fine-grained evaluation reveals systematic model biases: all methods perform better on static descriptions than dynamic ones, enabling targeted future research
Ablation studies show practical value of motion: +1.6% J&F improvement with just one motion frame, encouraging exploration of motion-enhanced long-video understanding
Clear presentation with comprehensive statistics, well-designed figures, and logical organization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of ReferMo: primarily combines existing components (Swin Transformer, ReferDINO, SAM2, MPEG-4 motion vectors) without significant methodological innovation; motion encoding approach uses standard MPEG-4 technique

Questionable comparison fairness: ReferMo only performs language-guided reasoning on keyframes while using SAM2 for non-keyframe propagation, whereas baseline Transformer methods perform vision-language fusion on all frames—this architectural difference makes direct comparison problematic and unclear whether improvements stem from motion or from reduced supervision

Critical gap in analysis: Table 2 shows all methods achieve nearly identical tIoU (~68-72) despite 18-point J&F variance, suggesting temporal consistency is NOT the bottleneck—yet the paper emphasizes new temporal metrics. This undermines the motivation for tIoU and vIoU and leaves their utility questionable

Insufficient investigation of baseline failures: SAM2-based methods (VideoLISA, GLUS, SAMWISE) dramatically underperform (33-36 J&F), but only brief speculation is provided; no analysis of why methods designed for video tracking fail on this benchmark

Missing annotation quality metrics: no inter-annotator agreement scores, expertise level of 20 college annotators unclear, and no final quality statistics provided despite iterative check-correct workflow

Dataset composition bias inadequately addressed: heavily human-centric (71.9% humans, 12.7% animals, 15.4% instruments) with potential limited generalization to non-human domains; no discussion of limitations or mitigation strategies

Training setup raises fairness concerns: all baselines trained for only 6 epochs with hyperparameters following ReferDINO defaults—not optimized for individual methods; no exploration of whether longer training or tuning could improve baselines

Lacks comprehensive error analysis: no qualitative failure cases, no breakdown by challenge type (occlusion vs. disappearance vs. shot changes), no analysis of performance by object duration or description type difficulty
Limited cross-dataset validation: no comparison with LVOS benchmark mentioned in related work; no analysis of transfer from short-video to long-video datasets

Incomplete technical justification: motion at H/16×W/16 resolution impact on small objects unexplored; edge case handling in metric definitions (both empty predictions) not discussed; SAM2 version and exact mask generation settings not fully specified

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in RVOS research by introducing the first large-scale long-form video benchmark (2,193 videos, 60+ seconds), filling a real need as existing datasets are limited to short clips

Dataset is well-constructed with substantial scale (36.7 total hours, 2.1M masks, 163 object classes) and multi-source diversity, with rigorous quality control through iterative check-correct workflow
Novel contribution of three text description types (static, dynamic, hybrid) enabling fine-grained evaluation and revealing model biases toward static attributes
Introduction of temporal (tIoU) and volumetric (vIoU) metrics addresses legitimate gap—existing frame-wise metrics ignore temporal consistency, which is important for real-world applications
Comprehensive benchmarking of 6 SOTA methods clearly demonstrates their degradation on long-form scenarios, establishing dataset difficulty and importance
Clear problem formulation and well-articulated motivation for why long-term RVOS is challenging and practically important
weaknesses: Critical lack of quantitative analysis of dataset properties: despite claiming objects undergo occlusion, disappearance-reappearance, and shot changing, no statistics provided on frequency, duration, or distribution of these phenomena—essential for understanding dataset characteristics

Baseline method (ReferMo) demonstrates weak novelty: combines standard components (MPEG-4 motion, deformable attention, cross-attention, Hungarian matching) without algorithmic innovation; improvement primarily from adding motion frames rather than novel architectural insights

Unfair experimental comparison: ReferMo only predicts keyframes with frozen SAM2 handling other frames, while competitors predict end-to-end; this offloads difficulty to pretrained tracker and violates fair comparison principle
Train-test mismatch: training uses 6 clips with 3-frame motion but inference uses actual clips with up to 11 frames; this discrepancy is not discussed or analyzed

Proposed evaluation metrics have significant validation gaps: tIoU measures frame presence overlap (potentially gameable by predicting empty), vIoU only averages over temporal intersection (asymmetric, incentivizes false negatives); no validation against human quality judgments

Dataset construction introduces systematic biases: SAM2-generated masks with manual correction may bias models toward SAM2's segmentation style; limited annotator diversity (20 students) with no inter-annotator agreement reported; small validation team (3 experts) for 2.1M masks

Insufficient explanation of dramatic performance degradation: SAM2-based methods SOTA on short videos perform poorly on Long-RVOS (35.6 vs 51.3 J&F), but explanation is superficial; no deeper investigation of why tracking degrades in long-video scenarios

Limited ablation studies: only two ablations (keyframes vs full video, motion length); missing ablations on multi-modal fuser, dual attention, global interaction components, and analysis of description-type specific performance

Heavy object bias: 71.9% human instances raises generalization concerns for animals (12.7%) and instruments (15.4%); no analysis of whether models transfer across object categories or maintain balanced performance

No validation of metric properties or gaming robustness: asymmetric vIoU definition and conservative prediction encouragement in tIoU not discussed; metrics not benchmarked against human perceptual quality

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in RVOS: first minute-level benchmark for long-term video segmentation with 2,193 videos averaging 60+ seconds, vs. existing datasets limited to 1-15 seconds

High-quality dataset construction with rigorous annotation workflow: iterative check-correct cycles with SAM2-based refinement, expert validation, and no artificial text augmentation resulting in 24,689 authentic descriptions

Novel contribution of tIoU and vIoU metrics for temporal and spatiotemporal consistency evaluation, addressing overlooked limitation of frame-wise metrics in handling occlusion and object disappearance

Comprehensive benchmarking of 6 SOTA methods revealing critical finding: SAM2-based methods (SOTA on short videos) fail catastrophically on long videos, indicating gains stem from tracking rather than language understanding

Substantial dataset diversity: 163 object classes, multiple video sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), balanced description types (35% static, 32.5% dynamic, 32.45% hybrid), and oracle analysis showing 25% performance gap to MeViS
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem statement, comprehensive statistics, and systematic evaluation protocol that will facilitate future research
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in ReferMo baseline: uses standard MPEG-4 keyframe extraction, conventional self-attention motion encoder, and simple gating fusion (Eqs. 3-4); primarily relies on SAM2 for non-keyframe tracking without methodological innovation

Insufficient ablation studies: missing ablations on fusion mechanisms, attention components, clip decomposition architecture, and keyframe selection strategies; only motion presence/length ablated despite acknowledging multiple design choices

SAM2 dependency obscures contribution quantification: oracle SAM2 achieves 52.8-54.5 J&F vs. ReferMo's 52.8 J&F, making unclear whether improvements stem from proposed method or tracking quality; upper bound analysis shows diminishing returns

Incomplete analysis of long-video failure modes: no systematic ablation by video length, object duration, occlusion frequency, or disappearance-reappearance patterns; limited qualitative failure case analysis

Dataset quality concerns: mask annotations rely heavily on SAM2 (inheriting potential biases); no quantitative quality metrics or inter-annotator agreement reported; text descriptions from 20 college students without expertise verification

Evaluation metrics lack novelty and validation: tIoU/vIoU are straightforward extensions of standard temporal/volumetric IoU; no validation that metrics correlate with human perception or downstream task performance; no robustness analysis

Experimental limitations reduce confidence: only 6 training epochs with no learning curves; no cross-dataset evaluation (Long-RVOS↔MeViS); hyperparameters follow ReferDINO defaults without long-video justification; small validation set (113 videos) without confidence intervals

Significant data bias and incomplete analysis: 71.9% human objects limits generalization claims; no class-wise performance breakdown; no statistical significance testing on results; potential distribution shifts between source datasets unanalyzed
Reproducibility gaps: project URL not provided; SAM2 refinement details vague; no dataset/code release timeline stated; supplementary motion extraction details promised but unavailable

strengths: Addresses clear gap in RVOS research: first minute-level benchmark for long-term video object segmentation, scaling from 4-13s to 60+ seconds on average with 2,193 videos and diverse annotations

Comprehensive dataset contribution: 2.1M pixel-level masks, 163 object classes, 24,689 carefully curated descriptions with three explicit types (Static/Dynamic/Hybrid), and rigorous multi-stage annotation with quality verification
Introduces useful new evaluation metrics (tIoU, vIoU) that address real limitations of frame-wise metrics for temporal consistency assessment in long videos with disappearance-reappearance patterns

Thorough experimental evaluation: benchmarks 7 SOTA methods fairly, provides fine-grained analysis by description type, comprehensive ablations, oracle analysis showing 25% performance gap, and robustness studies across occlusion rates

Diverse dataset construction from multiple sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D) ensuring variety in objects (163 classes), scenes (indoor/outdoor/egocentric), and description styles with balanced distribution
Clear demonstration that current SOTA methods significantly struggle in long-video scenarios, with comprehensive results showing method-dependent performance degradation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of baseline method: ReferMo combines existing techniques (MPEG-4 motion extraction from Video-LaVIT, standard spatial/channel gating, dual cross-attention, SAM2 tracking) without significant methodological innovation; local-to-global architecture is intuitive but not novel

Heavy dependence on SAM2: ReferMo only predicts keyframe masks while SAM2 provides temporal tracking; Table 4c shows SAM2 contributes 2.5-2.7 J&F (~5% of 52.9 total), making it difficult to isolate ReferMo's true contribution to long-video understanding

Concerningly low absolute performance raises questions about task formulation: ReferMo achieves 52.9 J&F overall vs. 80.6 J&F oracle on MeViS (shorter videos), with 25% gap between oracle and actual performance suggesting fundamental difficulty; very low vIoU scores (8-47) across all methods warrant investigation of metric design

Significant dataset bias not adequately mitigated: 71.9% human instances dominate; animals (12.7%) and instruments (15.4%) severely underrepresented; exclusion of background stuff classes mentioned only in supplementary material without justification, limiting generalization claims

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: paper shows models struggle but provides limited insight into root causes; large performance gap between Dynamic (49.3 J&F) vs. Static (55.8 J&F) descriptions unexplored; limited investigation of which long-video phenomena (long disappearances, view changes, occlusion sequences) are hardest

Dataset construction choices lack justification: >20 second threshold, 6-clip sampling, 3-frame motion vectors appear arbitrary without ablations or rationale; fair comparison concerns as existing methods trained on 4-8 frames but tested on all frames, while ReferMo trains on keyframes only

Evaluation metrics lack validation: tIoU remains 'relatively stable' across methods despite large J&F variation (suggesting possible lack of discriminative power); no discussion of metric correlation with perceptual quality; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Missing critical analyses: no inter-annotator agreement statistics for text annotations; no error mode analysis or qualitative failure cases; no annotation cost assessment; no discussion of practical applicability given low absolute performance levels; incomplete comparison to motion-focused MeViS (2023)

strengths: Addresses a clear gap: First large-scale long-term RVOS benchmark with 2,193 videos averaging 60+ seconds, substantially longer than existing datasets (4-13s)
Well-constructed dataset with rigorous quality control: Multi-source integration, iterative check-correct annotation workflow, balanced description types, 163 object classes

Useful new evaluation metrics: tIoU and vIoU capture temporal consistency, revealing that high J&F doesn't guarantee temporal consistency (Table 3 demonstrates significant performance variation across metrics)
Comprehensive benchmarking: 7 SOTA methods evaluated with detailed ablations, analysis across occlusion rates, description types, and event complexity
Practical relevance: Dataset incorporates realistic challenges (occlusion, disappearance-reappearance, shot changes, 60%+ videos with multiple events)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations demonstrating dataset properties and temporal challenges
weaknesses: Limited novelty in baseline method: ReferMo heavily borrows from ReferDINO (same backbone, dual cross-attention, Hungarian alignment, OTE module), with motion integration being the primary addition. Motion extraction via MPEG-4 is from Video-LaVIT [20], and image-motion fusion (Eq. 3-4) uses standard gating mechanisms—overall contribution is incremental

Modest performance improvements with experimental fairness concerns: ReferMo gains only +4-5 J&F over ReferDINO; oracle analysis shows SAM2 alone achieves 54.3-56.6 J&F, competing with ReferMo's 52.9 J&F, suggesting improvements may derive from SAM2 tracking rather than novel reasoning. Crucially, ReferMo uses different supervision (keyframe-only vs full-frame), conflating motion information contribution with sparse supervision effects; missing ablation where ReferDINO is trained with identical supervision

Insufficient analysis of temporal understanding challenges: Despite introducing temporal metrics, paper lacks deep investigation into why temporal reasoning fails. Dynamic descriptions show 49.3 J&F vs 55.8 for Static (6.5 point gap), yet no analysis of motion understanding bottlenecks. Multi-event performance drops from 52.9 to 40.5 J&F with no investigation of which temporal phenomena are problematic. No error analysis or failure case characterization provided

Critical missing cross-dataset validation: No evaluation of transfer learning to MeViS, Refer-YouTube-VOS, or other benchmarks. All results use Long-RVOS training/testing only. For a benchmark paper, this is a major gap—generalization and transferability are unknown

Metric design limitations: tIoU (Eq. 1) measures only frame index overlap without penalizing spatial quality differences; vIoU (Eq. 2) only sums over frame intersection, potentially underweighting false positives/negatives. No justification for why these designs are optimal or comparison to alternative temporal consistency metrics

Significant dataset limitations: Heavy human bias (71.9% humans, 12.7% animals) severely limits generalizability; small test set (226 videos, 9.3% of total) reduces metric confidence; no inter-annotator agreement reported for text quality; lacks background stuff classes as acknowledged; no analysis of underrepresented object/scenario categories

Unexplained method design choices: Why MPEG-4 motion over optical flow without empirical comparison? Why 6 clips and 3-frame motion vectors (appear arbitrary)? Why predict only on keyframes for long-term understanding—doesn't this lose frame-level dynamics? Why rely on pretrained SAM2 rather than end-to-end training, making attribution ambiguous?

Table 5 contradiction: Global interaction alone adds only +0.2 J&F while motion adds +1.1 J&F, contradicting the 'local-to-global' architectural framing. This suggests the local processing dominates, raising questions about the method's core design

Limited investigation of method specifics: Table 6 shows ReferMo maintains advantages under occlusion but mechanism is unclear—is improvement from motion, sparse supervision, or specific architecture? No causal analysis provided. Why do SAM2-based methods underperform existing SOTA on Long-RVOS despite superior short-video results? Paper doesn't investigate

Reproducibility and clarity gaps: Empty 'Project Page' link, critical implementation details in supplementary material, SAM2 version specificity (why specifically 'sam2.1 hiera large'?), dataset release timeline unclear, motion extraction at 748 FPS mentioned without validation details

strengths: Addresses a clear and practical gap: existing RVOS datasets focus on short videos (4-13s), while this work provides 2,193 videos averaging 60+ seconds with comprehensive annotations, representing a significant scale increase critical for real-world applications

High-quality, large-scale dataset: 2.1M pixel-level masks with rigorous SAM2-based annotation and iterative quality control, 24,689 authentic descriptions (no synthetic augmentation), 163 object categories from diverse sources, balanced representation across Static/Dynamic/Hybrid description types

Novel evaluation metrics addressing real limitations: tIoU and vIoU capture temporal consistency, effectively demonstrating that frame-wise J&F scores do not correlate with temporal robustness—a blind spot in prior evaluation protocols

Comprehensive and insightful benchmarking: 7 SOTA methods evaluated, oracle analysis reveals fundamental task difficulty (SAM2 achieves only 54-56 J&F vs 77-80 on MeViS), fine-grained analysis exposes systematic bias toward static attributes and weakness in dynamic understanding

Thoughtful dataset design: detailed annotation of video attributes (occlusion, disappearance-reappearance, view change), each video contains multiple objects (avg 3.4) reducing bias, Table 8 demonstrates Long-RVOS is substantially more challenging than prior work

Extensive experimental validation: multiple ablations isolating component contributions (Table 4-6), analysis across occlusion rates and event complexity, validation set consistency checks, qualitative comparisons demonstrating practical improvements
weaknesses: Incremental baseline method: ReferMo combines existing techniques (MPEG-4 decomposition, SAM2, dual cross-attention) with straightforward motion integration; lacks novelty in conceptual approach to long-term understanding and provides limited insights into why long-term RVOS is fundamentally challenging

Heavy dependence on SAM2 for non-keyframes: ReferMo only predicts on keyframes, with SAM2 handling remaining frames (contributing 2.5-2.7 J&F); limits applicability and obscures contribution of video-language reasoning vs. leveraging superior tracking; failure modes when SAM2 tracking breaks not analyzed

Limited analysis of failure modes and long-term challenges: While demonstrating methods struggle, paper provides insufficient investigation into specific causes (disappearance-reappearance vs. occlusion vs. long-range gaps); oracle analysis shows magnitude but not mechanisms; minimal qualitative failure analysis

Dataset biases not fully addressed: Heavy skew toward human instances (71.9%) may limit generalization; MPEG-4 compression biases not discussed; inter-annotator agreement for descriptions not reported; exclusion of background stuff classes acknowledged but limits scope

Motion extraction methodology underexplored: MPEG-4 motion vectors are coarse (16×16 macroblock resolution); alternatives (optical flow, learned motion) dismissed without comparison; ablation (Table 4b) shows motion helps (+1.1 J&F) but doesn't isolate what motion patterns matter most

ReferMo design choices lack justification: hyperparameter choices (6 clips, 3-frame motion vectors) not ablated; Hungarian algorithm for alignment and global interaction module simply reuses ReferDINO without exploring alternatives; limited architectural novelty

Evaluation metrics relatively simple: tIoU is binary (non-empty vs. empty) without soft boundaries; vIoU essentially averages per-frame J&F—modest novelty; no comparison with alternative temporal consistency metrics from literature

Missing critical experiments: No cross-dataset transfer learning analysis (does MeViS pretraining help or hurt?); limited investigation of why SAM2-based SOTA methods severely underperform on long videos; test set modest (226 videos) without confidence intervals or significance testing
